title: Linked genes: same genotype, different gametes
attribution: Original RecallWeave lesson. Scientific background: OpenStax Biology 2e §13.1, https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/13-1-chromosomal-theory-and-genetic-linkage ; NHGRI Linkage, https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Linkage ; NHGRI Crossing Over, https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Crossing-Over . All questions, explanations and examples are newly written; no textbook exercises or figures are reproduced.
license: CC0-1.0 applies to this original lesson text. Referenced sources retain their own licenses.

items.prompt: A plant is described only as AaBb. What does that genotype tell you about which alleles share a homologous chromosome?
options: A and B must be together, with a and b on the other homolog.
A and b must be together, with a and B on the other homolog.
Either arrangement is possible; the genotype alone does not specify the phase.
All four alleles must be together on one chromosome.
items.explanation: AaBb lists one copy of each allele at both loci. It does not say how the alleles are arranged across the two homologs. AB / ab is coupling; Ab / aB is repulsion. Both have genotype AaBb.
items.transfer: Write the two homolog pairs for AaBb. Check that each pair contains exactly one A, a, B and b.

items.prompt: Two AaBb plants have phases AB / ab and Ab / aB. In the ideal model, what changes when you switch between these phases while keeping the same recombination percentage?
options: The second plant becomes homozygous at both loci.
The parental gamete classes change, although the genotype remains AaBb.
The aabb tester must begin producing four types of gametes.
Every allele becomes more likely than its alternative.
items.explanation: Phase changes which allele combinations are parental: AB and ab in coupling, or Ab and aB in repulsion. Neither the parent's AaBb genotype nor the tester's ab gamete changes. Each single allele still has probability 1/2 under equal segregation.
items.transfer: At a recombination percentage below 50, predict which two gamete classes become more frequent after the phase switch.

items.prompt: An AaBb parent has homologs Ab / aB. Which pair is parental, meaning it preserves the combinations present on those homologs?
options: Ab and aB
AB and ab
Aa and Bb
AB and aB
items.explanation: The parental combinations are read directly from the homologs: Ab and aB. AB and ab recombine those combinations. Aa and Bb each contain two alleles of one locus, so neither is a gamete in this two-locus model.
items.transfer: For AB / ab, classify all four possible gametes again. Which labels switch category?

items.prompt: For AB / ab, suppose 20% of gametes are recombinant. Each parental class is equally likely, and each recombinant class is equally likely. What are P(AB) and P(Ab)?
items.explanation: The two parental classes share the remaining 80%, giving AB = ab = 40% = 2/5. The two recombinant classes share 20%, giving Ab = aB = 10% = 1/10. The percentage describes the total of a category, not the probability of each member.
items.transfer: Keep the same phase and change the recombinant total to 30%. Divide each category total between its two classes.

items.prompt: The lab is given a recombination percentage of 30. Which interpretation is used by its probability model?
options: The total probability of recombinant gametes is 3/10.
Exactly 30 crossover events occur in every 100 meioses.
The two loci are exactly 30 physical units apart on a chromosome.
Every group of ten offspring must contain exactly three recombinants.
items.explanation: The entered value stipulates a recombinant-gamete fraction. It is not an event count or a physical distance. Crossover events and the resulting gamete classifications are different quantities, and probabilities do not impose exact counts on finite samples.
items.transfer: Explain why you would need additional observations and assumptions before making an event-count or physical-distance claim.

items.prompt: The two parental gamete classes are equally likely. For Ab / aB with 0% recombinant gametes, which distribution follows the model? The order below is AB, Ab, aB, ab.
items.explanation: At zero recombination, the parental combinations Ab and aB each receive probability 1/2. The recombinant combinations AB and ab have probability zero. Equal allele segregation still holds: A versus a, and B versus b, each remain 1/2.
items.transfer: Use that distribution to add P(A) and P(B) separately. Unequal combination probabilities need not make individual alleles unequal.

items.prompt: In AaBb × aabb, the tester always contributes ab. If the AaBb parent contributes aB, what is the offspring genotype?
options: AaBb
aaBb
Aabb
aabb
items.explanation: Combine the contributions one locus at a time: a with a gives aa, and B with b gives Bb. The offspring is aaBb. The homozygous tester makes the other parent's gamete identifiable from the offspring genotype in this ideal model.
items.transfer: Map AB, Ab and ab through the same tester. Check that each gives a different offspring genotype.

items.prompt: The two parental gamete classes are equally likely. An AB / ab parent is testcrossed with aabb. Recombinant gametes total 40%, shared equally between their two classes. What is the probability of an aabb offspring?
items.explanation: The aabb offspring requires ab from the AaBb parent, because the tester also supplies ab. In coupling, ab is parental. The two parental classes share 60%, so P(ab) = P(aabb) = 30% = 3/10.
items.transfer: Switch to Ab / aB while retaining 40%. Is ab now parental or recombinant, and how does P(aabb) change?

items.prompt: The two recombinant gamete classes are equally likely. For Ab / aB × aabb with 20% recombinant gametes, what is P(AaBb), and how does it compare with the independent-assortment benchmark?
options: 2/5; it is above the 1/4 benchmark.
1/4; the genotype AaBb guarantees independent assortment.
1/5; each recombinant class gets the entire recombinant total.
1/10; it is below the 1/4 benchmark.
items.explanation: AaBb requires gamete AB. In repulsion, AB is recombinant and shares the 20% recombinant total with ab, so its probability is 10% = 1/10. The independent benchmark assigns 1/4 to each of the four combinations. A parent genotype alone cannot justify that benchmark.
items.transfer: Find P(Aabb) for the same cross. Explain why it lies on the other side of the benchmark.

items.prompt: At 50% recombination, both phases give AB, Ab, aB and ab probability 1/4 each. What can this equality establish by itself?
options: The loci must lie on different chromosomes.
The loci must be adjacent on the same chromosome.
The distribution matches independent assortment, but does not establish chromosome location.
Crossing over has stopped.
items.explanation: The four equal probabilities match the independent-assortment distribution. They do not uniquely locate the loci: loci on different chromosomes and sufficiently separated loci on the same chromosome can appear unlinked. The lab reports distribution equality, not a chromosome-location test.
items.transfer: Separate two claims in your own words: 'these probabilities match' and 'these genes are on different chromosomes'.

items.prompt: A modeled offspring genotype has probability 1/10. A learner says, 'If I collect ten offspring, exactly one must have that genotype.' What is the best correction?
options: Exactly one is guaranteed only if the parental phase is coupling.
One is the expected count, but the actual count in ten offspring can differ.
The probability must be changed to match the first ten observations.
Probability 1/10 means the genotype cannot appear before the tenth offspring.
items.explanation: For ten offspring with the stated probability, the expected count is 10 × 1/10 = 1. That is an average over repeated samples, not a quota for each sample. Finite data can deviate without invalidating the probability model.
items.transfer: Would observing zero in one sample of ten prove that the modeled probability is zero? Explain the difference between a possibility and a guarantee.

items.prompt: In an ideal testcross, the AaBb parent's gamete contributions are inferred as AB: 41, Ab: 9, aB: 11, ab: 39. Assuming the lab's equal-segregation and no-survival-bias model is appropriate, which interpretation is best supported?
options: The pattern is consistent with coupling and an observed recombinant fraction of 20/100; it does not prove an exact underlying fraction or physical distance.
The 41 versus 39 difference proves that one allele fails to segregate.
The genes must be on different chromosomes because all four classes occurred.
There must have been exactly twenty crossover events.
items.explanation: AB and ab are the more frequent pair, consistent with coupling under the stated model. The other pair contributes 9 + 11 = 20 of 100 observations. This observed fraction is an estimate, not proof of an exact underlying probability, a count of crossover events, or a physical map distance.
items.transfer: Before interpreting an unfamiliar dataset, ask how the gamete contributions were identified and whether differential survival or segregation distortion could affect the counts.
